\section[la tarea]{la tarea — the task; homework}

\label{lesson:ES-C593-tarea}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the head office, then the Spanish for the branch.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la tarea}
\textbf{la tarea} — \textquotedblleft{}the task; homework\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi tarea es hablar con los clientes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My task is to talk to the customers.}
\end{quote}

In Latin America \emph{la tarea} is also school homework; Spain says \emph{los deberes}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tarea} was borrowed from Andalusian Arabic \emph{ṭaríḥa}, a set amount of work (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la tarea}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la tarea}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la tarea}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the head office, then the Spanish for the branch, then say \emph{la tarea} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la tarea mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The task; homework\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[desempeñar]{desempeñar — to carry out, to perform; to hold (a post)}

\label{lesson:ES-C593-desempenar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the branch, then the Spanish for the task.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desempeñar}
\textbf{desempeñar} — \textquotedblleft{}to carry out, to perform; to hold (a post)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Desempeña un papel importante en la empresa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She plays an important role in the company.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Desempeñar un cargo} — to hold a post.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desempeñar} is built on \emph{empeñar} 'to pawn' with \emph{des-}. \emph{Empeñar} goes with \emph{empeño} 'a pledge', which EtymDB traces to Latin \emph{in pignus} 'in pledge'. To redeem a pledge became to carry out a duty.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desempeñar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desempeñar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{desempeñar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the branch, then the Spanish for the task, then say \emph{desempeñar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does desempeñar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To carry out, to perform; to hold (a post)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el rendimiento]{el rendimiento — the performance, the output; the yield}

\label{lesson:ES-C593-rendimiento}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the task, then the Spanish for to carry out.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el rendimiento}
\textbf{el rendimiento} — \textquotedblleft{}the performance, the output; the yield\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Su rendimiento en el trabajo es excelente.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Her performance at work is excellent.}
\end{quote}

\emph{El rendimiento escolar} — performance at school.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rendimiento} is built on \emph{rendir} with \emph{-miento} (EtymDB); \emph{rendir} is inherited from spoken Latin \emph{rendere}, Latin \emph{reddere} 'to give back'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[dedicarse]{dedicarse — to do for a living; to devote oneself}

\label{lesson:ES-C593-dedicarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to carry out, then the Spanish for the performance.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dedicarse}
\textbf{dedicarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to do for a living; to devote oneself\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
¿A qué te dedicas?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{What do you do for a living?}
\end{quote}

\emph{¿A qué te dedicas?} is the usual way to ask about someone's job. Spelling: \emph{me dediqué}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dedicarse} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{dedicare} 'to devote, to dedicate', built on \emph{dicare} 'to proclaim', a relative of \emph{dicere} 'to say' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dedicarse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{dedicarse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to carry out, then the Spanish for the performance, then say \emph{dedicarse} again

\section[eficiente]{eficiente — efficient}

\label{lesson:ES-C593-eficiente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the performance, then the Spanish for to do for a living.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: eficiente}
\textbf{eficiente} — \textquotedblleft{}efficient\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Es una trabajadora muy eficiente.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She is a very efficient worker.}
\end{quote}

The same for both genders.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{eficiente} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{efficiens} 'bringing about' (EtymDB), from \emph{efficere}, built from \emph{ex} and \emph{facere} 'to make'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the performance, then the Spanish for to do for a living, then say \emph{eficiente} again
